Description_Simple:
**Title:** Find the Top Three Largest Valid Integers from Standard Input

**Main Goal:**  
The program reads up to 10 integers from standard input (ignoring blank lines and any values outside the range `0` to `10,000`), stores the valid ones in an array, and then determines the three largest values. It finally prints those three values in descending order, one per line.

**How It Works:**  
- It initializes constants: an array size of `10`, a minimum valid value of `0`, and a maximum valid value of `10,000`.  
- A loop reads input lines, parses them as integers, and keeps only values in the range `[0, 10000]`.  
- A second pass over the stored numbers tracks the largest, second-largest, and third-largest values using a simple shift/update logic.  
- The helper methods (`lIIllIl`, `IllIlIl`, `IlIllIl`, `lllIlIl`, `IIIllIl`) are obfuscated equivalents of comparison/null/empty checks (`>=`, `<`, `>`, `!= null`, `!= 0`).
Description_Detailed: The program reads up to ten non‑negative integers from standard input, accepting only values between 0 and 10000 (it ignores invalid input, negative numbers, values larger than 10000, and stops on a blank line or EOF). It then computes and prints the three largest valid values in descending order, one per line; if fewer than three valid numbers were read, the remaining output lines are 0.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated digit-count printer for the sum of two integers

Main goal: The program reads pairs of integers from standard input in a loop, adds each pair together, and prints the number of decimal digits in the resulting sum (for results from 1 up to 9,999,999 digits). The strings that are printed (“1” through “7”) are hidden by obfuscation and decrypted at runtime using DES, Blowfish, Base64 decoding, and XOR with a key. The helper class FastScanner is a fast, byte-buffered input parser providing hasNext(), next(), nextInt(), nextLong(), and nextDouble(), although the visible main loop uses java.util.Scanner instead.
Description_Detailed: This Java program reads integers from standard input and processes them in pairs. In a loop it repeatedly reads two ints, computes their sum, then checks that sum against a series of numeric thresholds and prints one of several stored text labels for the matching interval. The checks are independent `if` statements, so several labels can be printed when intervals overlap, and one branch contains contradictory bounds so it never executes. A second class, `FastScanner`, is defined but never used, so it is just noise. In short: it is a simple interval classifier that maps each pair `a, b` to output text based on the value of `a + b`.

Description_Simple:
Title: Right-angled triangle verifier

Main goal: The program reads an integer N (number of test cases) from standard input, then reads N lines each containing three integers. For every triple it checks whether the values are in the range 1–100. If they are not, it records a “NO”-style verdict. Otherwise it sorts the three numbers, identifies the largest as the potential hypotenuse, and tests whether the Pythagorean theorem holds (largest² == sum of the other two squares). It outputs the corresponding verdict for each test case (effectively “YES” for a right triangle, “NO” otherwise). The obfuscated helper methods simply decrypt hard-coded string literals at runtime using DES, XOR and Blowfish, and provide comparison utilities.
Description_Detailed: The program reads a positive integer N from standard input, then reads up to N subsequent lines. Each line is split into three integer side lengths. If any side is outside the range 1–100, the program records "NO". Otherwise it orders the three values so the largest is treated as the hypotenuse and checks the Pythagorean condition: largest² equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. If the condition holds, it records "YES"; otherwise it records "NO". It stops reading after collecting N results and prints each recorded answer on its own line.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** GCD and LCM Pair Calculator

**Main Goal:** The program reads pairs of `long` integers from standard input and, for each pair, prints the **greatest common divisor (GCD)** followed by the **least common multiple (LCM)**.

**How it works:**
- It loops while input is available, reading two numbers per iteration.
- It computes the LCM by repeatedly adding the larger number until the result is divisible by the smaller one.
- If one number divides the other, that divisor is the GCD; otherwise it searches downward from half of the smaller number to find the largest value that divides both.
- The small helper methods are obfuscated wrappers for basic comparisons: `> 0`, `< 0`, `== 0`, and `!= 0`, plus a three-way `long` comparator.
Description_Detailed: The program reads pairs of 64-bit integers from standard input and, for each pair, prints two values separated by a space: the greatest common divisor (GCD) followed by the least common multiple (LCM). It scans multiples of the larger number to find one divisible by the smaller number, yielding the LCM, and then scans downward from half of the smaller number to find a common divisor, yielding the GCD. If the two input numbers are equal, it simply prints that number twice.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Standard Input Line Reverser

**Main goal:** The program reads lines from standard input and prints each line with its character order reversed.

**Functions / behavior:**
- The static initializer sets up a tiny integer constant array (used as loop bounds/offsets) and an obfuscated empty-string constant.
- `lIIIIIlIlIl(String encoded, String key)` decodes a Base64 string and XORs it with the repeating key (`yOrwo`). Here it is called with an empty Base64 input, producing the empty string used for the final `println`.
- `main(...)` opens `System.in`, reads one line at a time until EOF, reverses each line in place by swapping characters symmetrically around the center, then prints the reversed line followed by a newline.
- The other small helper methods (`IllIIIlIlIl`, `lIlIIIlIlIl`, `IIlIIIlIlIl`) are just obfuscated `>=`, `<`, and `!=` comparisons used to control the loops.

In short: it is an obfuscated line-reversal utility.
Description_Detailed: The program reads lines from standard input until end-of-file. For each line, it reverses the characters in place by swapping symmetric positions around the center, then prints the reversed line to standard output followed by a newline. It is a simple line-by-line text reverser.

Description_Simple:
<Title>Compound-Growth Calculator with Rounded-Up 5% Interest and Custom Fast Input</Title>

<Main Goal>
The program reads an integer `N` from standard input and computes a final monetary amount. It starts with `100000.0` and, in a loop, applies the update:

`amount = Math.ceil((amount + amount * 0.05) / 1000.0) * 1000.0`

which is equivalent to adding 5% interest and rounding the result up to the next multiple of 1000. The loop counter is initialized to the obfuscated constant `38`, so the update runs `max(0, N - 38)` times; the final value is printed as an integer.

<Key Functions>
- `main`: reads `N` using the custom scanner, runs the growth loop, and prints the result.
- `IIIlIllIIIl`: helper returning `a < b`.
- `lllIIllIIIl`: static initializer that sets the obfuscated loop-start constant.
- `IO`: a nested, buffered fast-input class that reads bytes from `System.in`, skips whitespace, and parses `long`/`int` values via `nextLong()` and `nextInt()`.
</Key Functions>
Description_Detailed: The program reads a single integer `N` from standard input. It starts with an amount of `100000` and repeats `N` times: multiply the current amount by `1.05` (a 5% increase), then round the result up to the nearest multiple of `1000`. After the loop, it prints the final amount as an integer. The `IO` inner class is simply a fast byte-based input scanner used to read the integer.

Description_Simple:
Title: Swap-Based Permutation Inverse

Main goal: This obfuscated Java program reads an integer N (number of items), an integer M (number of swaps), and M pairs of integers (a, b). It starts with items labeled 1 through N in order, then repeatedly swaps the labels a and b wherever they occur. After all swaps, it prints, for each label k from 1 to N, the 1-based position where label k currently resides — i.e., it outputs the inverse of the resulting permutation.
Description_Detailed: The program reads from standard input an integer `N`, an integer `M`, and then `M` lines each containing two integers. It treats each pair as a transposition applied in order to `N` items labeled `1` through `N`. Starting with each position holding its own label, it walks through every pair: whenever the current label equals one of the two numbers, it is replaced by the other. After all pairs are processed, the array holds the final label at each position. Finally, for each value `v = 1, 2, ..., N`, it prints the position (1-indexed) where `v` ended up. In other words, it computes the permutation produced by the sequence of swaps and outputs its inverse. Invalid input causes an error message to be printed to standard error.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Step-by-Step Insertion Sort Trace

**Main Goal:** The program reads an integer `n` and an array of `n` integers, then performs an insertion sort on the array. After each pass of the insertion sort, it prints the current state of the array, including the initial unsorted state and the final sorted state.
Description_Detailed: The program reads an integer N, then reads N integers into an array. It performs an insertion sort on the array, printing the contents of the array before each insertion pass (which includes the initial array as the first printed line). After the sort completes, it prints the final sorted array.

Description_Simple:
Title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) Calculator

Main goal: The program reads two integers from a single line of standard input and prints their greatest common divisor (GCD).

Summary: The code parses the input line into two integers, A and B. It then applies the Euclidean-identity step: if A < B it works with A and B % A; if A > B it works with B and A % B; if they are equal, it directly outputs A. It collects the divisors of each relevant value into two lists and finds their common divisors, finally printing the maximum common divisor, which is the GCD. The heavily obfuscated helper methods are simple comparison/predicate functions and a Base64/XOR string decoder that reconstructs the space character used to split the input line.
Description_Detailed: The program reads a single line of standard input containing two space-separated integers. It then enumerates the divisors of the two numbers (using one step of the Euclidean algorithm, i.e., reducing the larger number modulo the smaller), collects their common divisors into a list, and prints the largest common divisor. In other words, its real functionality is to compute and output the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the two input integers.

Description_Simple:
Title: Prime Number Counter via Trial Division

Main Goal: The program reads integers from standard input and counts how many of them are prime numbers (more precisely, numbers that are not divisible by any precomputed prime ≤ 10,000). It first builds a list of primes up to 100, then extends it to generate all primes up to 10,000. For each input number, it skips duplicates and excludes any value that is divisible by one of those precomputed primes (unless the number equals that prime). The final output is the count of remaining numbers, which equals the number of distinct primes in the input for the intended input range.
Description_Detailed: The program reads integers from standard input and counts how many distinct input values are prime numbers. It first builds a list of all primes less than 10,000 by trial division, seeded from the initial primes 2, 3, 5, and 7. For each input integer, it skips values already counted and tests whether the number is divisible by any of the precomputed primes, treating a match with a prime itself as not a divisibility failure. If no divisor is found, the value is added to the result set. Finally, it prints the size of that set. Because the divisibility check does not explicitly exclude 1, the value 1 is also counted, and composites whose only small factor exceeds 10,000 may be misclassified.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java Maximum Difference / Stock-Profit Calculator

Main Goal: The program reads an integer N followed by N integers from standard input and computes the maximum possible value of a later element minus an earlier element in that sequence (i.e., the largest gain from a single buy-then-sell transaction). It scans the numbers once, tracking the smallest value seen so far and the best difference found, then prints that maximum difference.

Summary: This is a heavily obfuscated/decompiled Java class. The static initializer sets up a small constant array used as indices. Many tiny helper methods simply wrap ordinary comparisons (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, null checks, etc.) and contain dead opaque branches to confuse readers. The main method uses a BufferedReader to read N and the N integer values, then iterates through the array to maintain a running minimum and the maximum difference between the current value and that minimum, finally outputting the result.
Description_Detailed: The program reads from standard input an integer `N` on the first line, followed by `N` integers (one per line). It then computes the maximum value of `arr[j] - arr[i]` for all pairs where `j > i` — that is, the largest increase from an earlier element to a later one. It tracks the smallest value seen so far and keeps updating the best difference, effectively solving the classic “maximum single-transaction stock profit” problem. Finally, it prints that maximum difference.

Description_Simple:
Title: Bubble Sort with Swap Counter

Main Goal: The code reads a list of integers from standard input, sorts them in ascending order using the bubble sort algorithm, then prints the sorted numbers separated by spaces followed by the total number of swaps performed during the sort.
Description_Detailed:
This program reads an integer `n` followed by `n` integers from standard input, sorts them using a bubble-sort-like algorithm, and outputs the sorted sequence along with the total number of adjacent swaps performed.

The algorithm repeatedly scans the array from the end toward the start, swapping any adjacent pair where the later element is smaller than the previous one. It continues making passes until a complete scan finds no out-of-order pair, at which point the array is sorted. A counter tracks every swap executed during these passes.

The sorted numbers are then printed in order, separated by a single space, followed by a newline and the total swap count.

The `FastScanner` class is a minimal custom reader for fast integer input from `System.in`.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Selection Sort with Swap Counter

**Main Goal:**  
This Java program reads an integer `n` and an array of `n` integers from standard input, sorts the array using the **selection sort** algorithm, and counts how many element swaps are performed during the sort. It finally prints the sorted array and the swap count.

**Key Functions:**
- `main(...)`: Reads input, executes selection sort, and outputs results.
- `parseArray(...)`: Converts the sorted integer array into a space-separated string for printing.
- `FastScanner`: A custom fast input reader supporting `nextInt()`, `nextLong()`, etc.
- Obfuscation helpers: Encrypted string constants and numeric arrays generated by the decompiler/copyright obfuscator.
Description_Detailed: This Java program reads an integer `N` followed by `N` integers from standard input. It then sorts the array in ascending order using a simple selection sort. While sorting, it counts how many times the minimum element of the remaining unsorted suffix is not already at the current position (i.e., how many non-trivial swaps occur). Finally, it prints the sorted array as space-separated values on one line and the swap count on the next line.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) Arithmetic Expression Evaluator

**Main Goal:**  
Read a single line of standard input containing a postfix arithmetic expression (integer operands and the operators `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` separated by spaces), evaluate it using a stack, and print the final integer result.

**How it works:**  
- The `Stack` class implements a basic integer stack with `push`, `pop`, `isEmpty`, `isFull`, and `initialize` methods.  
- `Main` scans the input string character by character.  
- When it encounters a sequence of digits, it builds the corresponding integer and pushes it onto the stack.  
- When it encounters an operator, it pops the top two values, applies the operator (`second-from-top op top`), and pushes the result back.  
- Spaces are ignored.  
- After processing the whole line, the final value left on the stack is printed.
Description_Detailed: This Java program evaluates a postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) arithmetic expression read from standard input. It reads a single line, scans its characters, and accumulates consecutive digit characters into integer operands, pushing each operand onto a stack. When it encounters one of the operators `+`, `-`, `*`, or `/`, it pops the top two stack values, applies the operator to them (the first popped value is the right-hand operand, the second is the left-hand operand), and pushes the result back onto the stack. Any spaces or other non-operator characters are simply skipped. After processing the entire input line, the program pops the final value from the stack and prints it. The core algorithm is a standard stack-based evaluator for integer postfix expressions.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Round-Robin CPU Process Scheduler

**Main Goal:**  
The program reads multiple test cases from standard input. For each test case it receives:
- `n` – the number of processes,
- `q` – the CPU time quantum,

followed by `n` lines each containing a process name and its required running time. It then simulates a **Round-Robin (RR) scheduling algorithm** and prints, for every process in completion order, its name followed by the clock time at which it finishes.

**How it works:**
1. All processes are stored in an array of `Process` objects.
2. The scheduler repeatedly visits processes in a circular fashion.
   - If a remaining time is `0`, the slot is skipped.
   - If a remaining time is **less than or equal to** `q`, the process finishes now; the elapsed time is increased by that remaining time and the result is printed.
   - Otherwise, the process runs for one quantum `q`, its remaining time is decreased by `q`, and the elapsed time is increased by `q`.
3. The program also removes already-finished processes from the array when too many empty slots have accumulated (a small optimization).
4. The loop continues until input is exhausted (`Scanner.hasNext()` returns false).

In short, this Java code is an obfuscated implementation of a Round-Robin scheduler that outputs process finish times.
Description_Detailed:
The program implements a round-robin CPU scheduling simulator. It reads test cases from standard input until EOF. Each test case starts with two integers, `n` (number of processes) and `q` (time quantum), followed by `n` process entries consisting of a name and a burst time.

It processes the jobs in cycles. For each process it allocates at most `q` time units. If the process’s remaining burst time is less than or equal to `q`, the process finishes, and the program prints its name followed by its total completion time. Otherwise, the process’s remaining time is reduced by `q`, total elapsed time advances by `q`, and the scheduler moves on to the next process. This repeats until every process has completed. The output lines record the processes’ finishing times in the order they finish.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Obfuscated Java Membership/Intersection Counter

**Main Goal:**  
The program reads two integer arrays from standard input and counts how many elements of the second (shorter) array are present in the first (longer) array.

**What it does:**
- `main` reads a length, a line of integers, then another length and another line of integers. The input lines are split using encrypted delimiter strings (decrypted via DES/Blowfish helpers).
- `method` ensures the first array is the longer one, then treats it as a sorted array divided into four parts by indices at ¼, ½, and ¾ of its length.
- For each value in the shorter array, it compares the value against those partition elements, selects the corresponding segment, and scans that segment linearly for an exact match.
- Every match increments a counter, which is finally printed.

**Key functions:**
- `lllIIllIlIIl` / `IIIlIllIlIIl`: decrypt Base64 strings using DES/Blowfish with MD5-derived keys (obfuscated delimiter strings).
- `IlIlIllIlIIl` / `lIIlIllIlIIl`: initialize the obfuscated integer constants and encrypted string constants.
- `lIllIllIlIIl`, `llIlIllIlIIl`, `IIllIllIlIIl`: wrappers for `==`, `<`, and `>` comparisons.
- `method`: performs the membership search/counting logic.
Description_Detailed:
This program reads two integer sequences from standard input and counts how many values from the second sequence are present in the first.

Input format:
- An integer N, followed by a line with N integers.
- An integer M, followed by a line with M integers.

The program stores the two integer arrays. Inside `method`, it makes the first array the larger one (swapping if necessary) and treats it as a sorted lookup table. It divides that table into four quarters using indices at one‑quarter, one‑half, and three‑quarters of its length. For each value in the second array, it compares the value with the boundary elements to decide which quarter could contain it, then linearly searches only that quarter. If an equal element is found, a counter is incremented. The final counter value is printed.

In short: it computes the number of elements from the second list that occur in the first list, using a quartile‑partitioned linear search on the first, larger list.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Population Standard Deviation Calculator

Main Goal: This Java program reads test cases from standard input and computes the population standard deviation for each one. For each case it reads an integer count n (stopping when n is 0), validates that n is within range and that the following line contains exactly n numeric values, then calculates sqrt( Σ(x − mean)² / n ) and prints each result.
Description_Detailed:
The program reads standard input in a loop until it receives a line containing exactly `0`. For each iteration, it reads an integer `n` and then a line of `n` space-separated integers. It validates that `n` is positive and does not exceed a preset maximum, and that the line actually contains `n` values. For each valid set, it computes the population standard deviation using the classic formula:

1.  Calculate the mean of the `n` integers.
2.  Sum the squared differences of each value from the mean.
3.  Divide that sum by `n` and take the square root.

The computed standard deviations are stored in an array, and after the terminating `0` is read, they are printed to standard output one per line using a formatted floating-point specifier. Invalid inputs stop further processing and suppress the output.

Description_Simple:

Main Goal:
The code reads an integer from standard input, validates that it is within the inclusive range [1, 100], and prints the cube (third power) of that number. If the input is not an integer or falls outside this range, it prints an exception stack trace.

Functions:

- `IlllIlIIlIIl`: Static helper that initializes the internal constant array with values 1 (minimum valid value) and 100 (maximum valid value).
- `llllIlIIlIIl`: Returns `true` if the first argument is greater than or equal to the second.
- `IIIIllIIlIIl`: Returns `true` if the first argument is strictly greater than the second.

Description_Detailed: The program reads a single line of input from standard input, parses it as a 32-bit signed integer, validates that it lies in the inclusive range 1 to 100, and prints the cube of that integer (n³). If the input cannot be parsed as an integer, falls outside the valid range, or an I/O error occurs, the program prints the corresponding exception's stack trace and exits without producing any numerical result. The obfuscation only hides the literal bounds 1 and 100 behind bit-shifted constants and adds spurious conditional branches that do not affect this core logic.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Rectangle Area and Perimeter Calculator

Main goal: The program reads two non-negative integers (typically a rectangle's width and height) from standard input and prints two values separated by a space: the product of the numbers and two times their sum. In other words, it computes `width * height` and `2 * (width + height)`. Under the obfuscation, the code uses a static constants array for hidden numeric/ASCII values, helper methods for simple comparisons, a loop that reads characters, stores decimal digits and counts per whitespace-delimited token, a loop that reconstructs those tokens into integers, and a final println that multiplies and sums the first two numbers.
Description_Detailed: The program reads one line from standard input, splitting it into whitespace-separated tokens. It parses the first two tokens as decimal integers (recognizing only the ASCII characters '0' and '1' as digits, so each token is a number made up solely of those digits). It then prints two values separated by a space: the product of the two integers and twice their sum. In other words, given side lengths a and b, it outputs the area a×b and the perimeter 2×(a+b) of a rectangle.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Java program to find the largest square-free integer ≤ N

Main goal: The program reads an integer N from standard input and prints the largest integer x ≤ N whose prime factorization has no repeated prime (i.e., x is square-free). If no such x > 1 is found, it prints 1.

How it works:
1. Static initialization builds obfuscated integer constants and decrypts obfuscated string literals using Blowfish, DES, and XOR helpers.
2. The `main` method first builds a smallest-prime-factor (SPF) table for numbers up to 1000 using a simple sieve.
3. Starting from N, it factorizes the current candidate using the SPF table and records each prime’s exponent in a HashMap.
4. It checks whether all prime exponents are equal. If they are all equal to 1, the candidate is square-free: it prints the candidate and exits.
5. Otherwise, it decrements the candidate and repeats until it falls below 2, then prints 1.

The many small helper functions are just obfuscated wrappers for comparisons (`==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, etc.) and arithmetic operations.
Description_Detailed:
The program reads a single integer \(n\) and finds the largest integer \(m \le n\) that is a perfect power with exponent at least 2 (i.e., every prime in its factorization appears with the same positive exponent \(e > 1\), so \(m = k^e\) for some integers \(k,e\) with \(e > 1\)).

It first builds a sieve of smallest prime factors up to 1000. Then it scans candidates downward from \(n\). For each candidate it divides repeatedly by its smallest prime factor, counting multiplicities in a hash map. It checks whether every counted prime has the same multiplicity; if that common multiplicity exceeds 1, it prints the candidate and exits. A short-circuit case also emits 2 when the scan reaches it, and if the scan finishes without finding such a number the program finally prints 1.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Integer Comparison with Input Validation

**Main Goal:**  
The program reads two integers from standard input. It first checks whether both numbers lie within the inclusive range `-1000` to `1480`. If either input falls outside the valid range, it prints an invalid-input/error message instead. The visible strings and constants are obfuscated: they are initialized and decrypted at runtime using Base64, XOR, DES, and Blowfish helpers.
Description_Detailed: The program reads two integers from standard input and validates that both are within the inclusive range -1000 to 1960. If the inputs are valid, it prints a message indicating whether the first number is less than, greater than, or equal to the second number. If either input falls outside the accepted range, it prints an out-of-range/error message instead.

Description_Simple:

Description_Detailed: The program reads an integer `n` and a string `s`, then counts how many times the consecutive three-character substring `"ABC"` occurs in `s`. It scans every starting position from `0` up to `n‑3`, checking whether `s[i]`, `s[i+1]`, and `s[i+2]` equal `'A'`, `'B'`, and `'C'` respectively, and increments a counter for each match. Finally, it prints the total count. The FastScanner/FastWriter classes and encrypted string tables are only obfuscated I/O helpers; they do not affect this core counting logic.

Description_Simple:

It uses a series of conditional comparisons (implemented through helper methods for less than, greater than, and equality) to determine the correct ordering among the three input numbers and outputs the result.
Description_Detailed: The program reads three integers from standard input, sorts them into non-decreasing (ascending) order, and prints the three sorted values separated by spaces. It handles all orderings of the three numbers, including cases where some values are equal, by selecting the appropriate permutation of the inputs and printing them as `a b c` such that `a <= b <= c`.

Description_Simple:
Title: Obfuscated Circle-in-Rectangle Validator

Main goal: This decompiled Java program reads one line from standard input, splits it into five integers (rectangle width, rectangle height, circle center x, circle center y, and radius), and checks whether the circle lies completely inside the axis-aligned rectangle. It uses four conditional blocks that verify the center is at least the radius away from each relevant rectangle side (covering different quadrant orientations). When a case matches it prints a success message such as "Yes"; if none match it prints "No". The code hides its string literals and simple comparisons behind runtime DES/Blowfish/Base64 string decryption and helper methods like lIlIlllIlIll (<=), IllIlllIlIll (>=), and IIIllllIlIll (==0).
Description_Detailed:
The program reads one line from standard input, splits it on whitespace, and parses five integers: `W`, `H`, `x`, `y`, and `r`. It then tests whether an axis-aligned circle of radius `r` centered at `(x, y)` lies completely inside the rectangle with corners `(0, 0)` and `(W, H)`. This is done by checking the four containment conditions:

- `x - r >= 0`
- `x + r <= W`
- `y - r >= 0`
- `y + r <= H`

If all conditions are true, it prints a “Yes” answer; otherwise it prints “No”. The extra conditional blocks, encrypted string constants, and decryption helper methods are obfuscation/dead code and do not change the core algorithm: a simple circle-inside-rectangle validation.

Description_Simple:
**Title:** Numbered Case Echo Program

**Main Goal:** This obfuscated Java program reads lines from standard input until it encounters a terminating sentinel string (the sentinel literals are stored encrypted and decrypted at runtime using DES with an MD5-derived key), collects up to 10,000 lines, and then prints each collected line prefixed with `Case N: `. The first loop performs the input reading and stops on the sentinel, while the second loop outputs the stored lines with incrementing case numbers. Helper methods handle initialization of constants, decryption of string literals, array bounds, and equality checks.

# Minimum Increments to Make Array Non-Decreasing Calculator

## Main Goal
This Java program reads an integer `n` and an integer array of size `n` from standard input, then computes and prints the **minimum total increase** required to make the array **non-decreasing** — meaning after modification, every element must be greater than or equal to the previous element.

## How It Works
1. **Input reading**: The obfuscated `Foster` class is a fast input scanner that reads `n` and the `n` integers.
2. **Prefix maximum computation**: It builds an auxiliary array where each position `i` stores the maximum value seen in the original array from index `0` to `i` (inclusive).
3. **Difference summation**: It sums the difference between each prefix maximum and the corresponding original array value. This total equals the smallest total amount that must be added to elements so that no element is smaller than its predecessor.

## Key Functions
- `main(...)`: Orchestrates input reading, computes the prefix maximum array, accumulates the total increments, and prints the result.
- `Foster.nextInt()` / `Foster.intArray(...)`: Read integers and arrays from standard input.
- `lIllllIIIIl(...)`: A helper comparison (`n < n2`) used in while-loops.

The rest of the code is obfuscated scaffolding, debugging utilities (`watch`, `print`, `println`), and encrypted string constants, but they do not affect the core computation.
Description_Detailed:
The program reads an integer `n` and an array `a` of `n` integers.

It computes the **running maximum from left to right** of the array, producing a sequence `m[i]` where `m[i] = max(a[0], a[1], ..., a[i])`.

Then it sums the differences between each running maximum and the original value:

```
total = Σ (m[i] - a[i])  for i = 0 … n-1
```

This total is the **minimum amount that must be added to the array elements** to make the sequence non-decreasing, because each element is raised to match the largest value seen so far.

Finally, the program prints this total.

**Title: Integer-to-Alphabet Bijective Base-26 Converter**

**Main Goal:**  
This Java program reads a positive `long` integer from standard input and converts it into a lowercase bijective base-26 string — the same numbering scheme used by Excel column titles, but using lowercase letters (e.g., `1 → "a"`, `26 → "z"`, `27 → "aa"`, `28 → "ab"`, etc.).

**How it works:**

1. **Determine output length** — It loops through possible lengths and uses geometric-series bounds (`26¹ + 26² + ... + 26ᴺ`) to find the correct number of letters for the input.

2. **Adjust to zero-based offset** — It subtracts the sum of all shorter strings (`26¹ + ... + 26ᴺ⁻¹`) so the remaining value maps cleanly to an `N`-digit base-26 number.

3. **Convert and pad** — The adjusted value minus one is converted to a base-26 string with `Long.toString(..., 26)` and padded with leading `"0"` characters to reach the computed length.

4. **Map digits to letters** — Each base-26 digit (characters `0‑9`, `a‑p`) is compared against an obfuscated lookup table of encrypted strings and replaced with the corresponding lowercase letter `a` through `z`.

5. **Obfuscation helpers** — The constant strings for the alphabet and digits are stored encrypted. The static initializer decrypts them at runtime using Base64, XOR, DES (with an MD5-derived key), and Blowfish (also MD5-derived).

In short, despite the obfuscated string decryption and decompiled variable names, the code is fundamentally a utility that maps an integer to its lowercase Excel-style column label.
Description_Detailed:
The program reads one signed 64-bit integer from standard input and prints its corresponding lowercase Excel-style column title.

It first finds the length `n` of the title by locating the block where the input falls: the sum of all shorter label counts must be strictly less than the input, and the sum including length-`n` labels must be at least the input. It then subtracts the count of all shorter labels and decrements by one to obtain a zero-based offset inside the length-`n` block. That offset is converted to base-26, padded on the left with zero digits to length `n`, and each base-26 digit is mapped to a lowercase letter (`0`→`a`, `1`→`b`, …, `9`→`j`, `a`→`k`, …, `p`→`z`). The resulting string is printed.

The encrypted string array, multiple decryption helpers, fake branches, and renamed variables only hide the digit strings and helper constants; the real logic is an obfuscated integer-to-column-title conversion.

- `x = 2*n - m/2`
- `y = m/2 - n`

Then it checks:
1. `n == x + y` and `m == 2*x + 4*y` — i.e., the inputs are arithmetically consistent.
2. `x >= 0` and `y >= 0` — i.e., the computed counts are non-negative.

If both hold, it prints an encrypted “yes/success” message; otherwise it prints an encrypted “no/error” message.

In short, this is a deobfuscated/competition-style Java program that answers whether a given `(count, total)` pair can be formed from items worth `2` and `4`.

The program is a command-line solver for the classic “chicken and rabbit” (heads-and-legs) problem. It reads two integers: the total number of heads `n` and the total number of legs `x`. It then computes:

- `chickens = 2*n - x/2`
- `rabbits = x/2 - n`

The outer `if` check is a disguised validation: it effectively verifies that `n == chickens + rabbits` and that `x` is even, which is required for a valid integer solution.

**Main Goal:**

```
f(1) = 1
f(n) = 2 * f(n / 2) + 1
```

Using integer division for `n / 2`, the result is equivalent to:

```
f(n) = 2^(floor(log2(n)) + 1) - 1
```

This value represents the number of nodes in a perfect binary tree with `floor(log2(n)) + 1` levels. The result is printed to standard output.

- **`solve()`**: Reads a long from input, seeds a memoization map with `(1, 1)`, and prints `dfs(n)`.
- **`dfs(long)`**: The core recursive function. If `n` is already memoized, it returns the cached value. Otherwise, it computes `2 * dfs(n / 2) + 1`, stores it in the `HashMap`, and returns it. Memoization avoids redundant recursive calls.
- **`FastScanner`**: A custom fast input-parsing inner class with methods like `nextInt()`, `nextLong()`, `nextDouble()`, `nextChar()`, `nextStr()`, `nextLine()`, and various array-reading helpers. It reads directly from a `BufferedReader` for speed, typical of competitive-programming solutions.
- **`ceil(long, long)`**, **`gcd(long, long)`**, **`lcm(long, long)`**: Mathematical utility methods defined in `Main` but not used by the actual solving logic.
- **Obfuscation artifacts**: The decompiled code contains many dead control-flow expressions (e.g., `"".length()` comparisons), an unused `MOD` field, and string-decryption scaffolding in `FastScanner`. These are byproducts of CFR decompilation and obfuscation and do not affect the core algorithm.

- `dfs(1) = 1`
- For `n > 1`: `dfs(n) = 2 * dfs(n / 2) + 1` (integer division)

Closed form: `dfs(n) = 2^(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1) − 1`, i.e. the Mersenne number made of all `1` bits whose length is one more than the position of the highest set bit of `n`. Equivalently, it is one less than twice the largest power of two not exceeding `n`.

Each non-zero prime factor is stored as a `[prime, exponent]` pair in its own `ArrayDeque`. If a remainder larger than `1` remains after trial division, it is also stored as a prime factor with exponent `1`.
4. **Sentinel termination**: A large sentinel prime (`100001`) is appended to both deques so the merge loop knows when both lists are exhausted.
5. **Merge / LCM computation**: The program repeatedly compares the current prime from each deque:
   - If the primes differ, it multiplies the running result by the prime that appears in only one list, raised to its exponent, and advances that list.
   - If the primes are equal, it multiplies by that prime raised to the **larger** of the two exponents (max exponent), then advances both lists.
   This merge computes the product of the maximum exponents across both factorizations, which is the definition of LCM.
6. **Output**: The accumulated product is printed.

**Helper functions:** The private methods (`IIlIlllIll`, `lIIllllIll`, `IllIlllIll`, etc.) are simple comparison wrappers for `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`, `>=`, and checking zero/non-zero values.

Any remaining unfactored portion of a number is stored as a single factor with exponent 1. The queues are terminated by a sentinel value (100001). The program then merges the two factor lists: for each distinct prime it uses the larger of the two exponents, and for primes present in only one number it uses that number's exponent. Multiplying these chosen prime powers together yields the LCM, which is output as a long integer.

**Main Goal:**  
This Java program reads a single string from standard input and determines how many pairs of symmetric characters differ, which equals the minimum number of character replacements needed to make the string a palindrome.

2. It splits the string into two halves. If the length is odd, the middle character is ignored.

This Java program reads a single whitespace-delimited token from standard input, compares it against a hidden list of seven predefined strings, and prints a numeric score based on the matching position (or `0` if the input is not in the list).

- **String Obfuscation**: The seven target strings are not stored as literals. They are encrypted and placed in a static `String[]` array (`IIIIlllIl`) inside a static initializer. Two decryption routines are used:
  - `lIIlIIIIlIl(...)` — Base64-decodes the ciphertext and XORs each character with a supplied key.

- **Search & Output**: The program loops through the seven strings. If the input equals one of them, it breaks out of the loop. It then prints `arrayLength - currentIndex`. Because the array length is `7`, a match at index `0` prints `7`, a match at index `6` prints `1`, and no match prints `0`.

- `FastReader` is a nested utility class that implements fast buffered input parsing with methods for `next()`, `nextInt()`, `nextLong()`, `nextDouble()`, `nextChar()`, and `nextLine()`, plus a `SpaceCharFilter` interface for customizing whitespace handling.

## Summary
In essence, this is a deliberately obfuscated lookup/rating tool: it secretly stores seven strings, asks the user for a string, and returns a rank from `7` down to `1` depending on which secret string matches, or `0` if none match. The heavy obfuscation (encrypted constants, bitwise-encoded integers, renamed variables) is intended to conceal the exact list of strings and the scoring logic from reverse engineering.
Description_Detailed: The program reads a single whitespace-delimited token from standard input and looks it up in a fixed array of seven decrypted strings: the three-letter English weekday abbreviations `SUN`, `MON`, `TUE`, `WED`, `THU`, `FRI`, `SAT` (in that order). Thus it maps `SUN` to `7`, `MON` to `6`, `TUE` to `5`, `WED` to `4`, `THU` to `3`, `FRI` to `2`, `SAT` to `1`, and prints `0` if the input token does not match any of them. **Main Goal:**  
Given a single positive integer `N` read from standard input, the program computes the minimum possible value of `a + b - 2` over all factor pairs `a × b = N` (with `a, b ≥ 1`). Equivalently, for every divisor `i` of `N` up to `√N`, it evaluates `i + N/i - 2` and keeps the smallest value. - For each divisor `i`, it computes `j = N / i`.
- If `i` exactly divides `N` (`N % i == 0`) and `i + j - 2` is smaller than the current answer, it updates `ans`.
- Finally, it prints `ans`.

`IlIllIlIIlIl(long, long)` returns `-1/0/1` for comparison, while `IIlllIlIIlIl`, `llIllIlIIlIl`, and `lIlllIlIIlIl` are wrapper Boolean checks for `== 0`, `≤ 0`, and `> 0`, respectively. These are used to express the loop and branching conditions in the obfuscated/decompiled code.

The smallest such value is tracked, starting from the trivial factorization `1 × N`, which gives `N - 1`. After scanning all divisors up to the square root, the program prints the minimum value found. In short, it computes

min_{a·b = N} (a + b - 2)

over all positive integer factorizations of `N`.

**Title:** Pairwise Product Sum Calculator

**Main Goal:**

\[
\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i \cdot a_j
\]

It calculates this using the identity:

\[
\left(\sum a_i\right)^2 - \sum a_i^2 = 2 \cdot \sum_{i<j} a_i a_j
\]

So it outputs `(totalSum * totalSum - sumOfSquares) / 2`.

**Input/Output Example:**  
Input:
```
3
1 2 3
```
Output:
```
11
```
Because `1*2 + 1*3 + 2*3 = 2 + 3 + 6 = 11`.

**Title:** Interval Intersection Length Calculator

**Main Goal:**  
This Java program reads a universe bound `n`, a count `m`, and `m` closed intervals `[a, b]`. It computes and prints the length of the common intersection of all those intervals within the initial range `[0, n]`. If the intervals do not overlap (their intersection is empty), it outputs `0`. For the special case `m == 1`, it directly outputs the length of the single interval (`b - a + 1`).

**How It Works:**
1. **Input:** Uses `Scanner` to read `n` and `m` from standard input.
2. **Initialization:** Creates an initial interval `[start, end] = [0, n]` and a result variable (`lllIIIIllIIlll`) set to `0`.
3. **Special Case (`m == 1`):** Reads one interval `[a, b]` and immediately computes `b - a + 1`.
4. **General Case (`m > 1`):** Loops `m` times, reading each interval `[a, b]` and updating `[start, end]` to reflect the intersection:
   - If `[a, b]` lies inside the current interval, shrink to `[a, b]`.
   - If the current interval lies inside `[a, b]`, keep it unchanged.
   - If they partially overlap on the right or left, adjust `start` or `end` accordingly.
   - If they are disjoint, set the result to `0` and stop.
   - The result is maintained as `end - start + 1`.
5. **Output:** Prints the final computed length.

**Helper Functions & Obfuscation:**  
The code is heavily obfuscated with similar-looking variable names (`I`, `l`, `Il`, etc.) and a static array `IllllIIIl` initialized through bitwise/XOR tricks. That array simply holds `[0, 1]`, used as constants. The helper methods are thin wrappers for comparisons:
- `IIIIIIllll(n, n2)` → `n == n2`
- `llIIIIllll(n, n2)` → `n >= n2`
- `lIIIIIllll(n, n2)` → `n < n2`
- `IlIIIIllll(n, n2)` → `n <= n2`

The `" ".length()` snippets are dead code that do not affect execution.
Description_Detailed: The program reads two integers, N and M, followed by M closed integer intervals [a, b]. It computes the length of the common intersection of all those intervals, using an initial reference interval of [0, N]. As each interval is read, the running intersection is narrowed: if the new interval lies inside the current one, the intersection becomes the new interval; if the current one lies inside the new one, it stays unchanged; if they overlap on the right, the left bound moves forward; if they are disjoint, the result is set to 0 and processing stops. A special case handles M = 1 by directly outputting b − a + 1 for the single interval. Finally, the program prints the size of the remaining common intersection (end − start + 1), or 0 if the intervals do not all overlap.

**Title:** Bitter Alchemy – Maximum Production Count from a Fixed Resource

**Main Goal:**

It computes the maximum total number of items that can be produced when each of the `N` given item types must be produced once (consuming `A[i]` resource per item), and any remaining resource is used to produce additional copies of the cheapest item type.

The answer is calculated as:
```
answer = N + (X - sum(A)) / min(A)
```
where `sum(A)` is the total resource needed to produce one of every item, and the leftover `(X - sum(A))` is divided by the smallest array element to obtain how many extra cheapest items can be made.

**Key Components:**
- `Main`: Entry point that connects `System.in`/`System.out` to the solver and starts the computation.
- `FastScanner`: A custom fast input scanner that reads bytes from standard input, skips whitespace, and parses `long`/`int` values and `int[]` arrays efficiently.

It sorts the array, computes `sum = Σ A[i]`, and identifies the smallest value `A[0]`.  
Then it outputs:

```
N + (X - sum) / A[0]
```

This corresponds to the classic greedy “all-you-can-eat” / “glutton” problem: Takahashi must eat each of the `N` dishes once (costing `sum` minutes total), then uses the remaining time `X - sum` to eat the cheapest dish as many additional times as possible. The result is the maximum total number of dishes he can eat within `X` minutes.

**Title:** Checker for feasible timed Manhattan-grid visits

**Main goal:**  
The code reads `n` triples `(t, x, y)` and decides whether a person starting at the origin `(0, 0)` at time `0` can be at each given `(x, y)` at the corresponding time `t`, moving on a grid at Manhattan speed at most `1`. It prints an encrypted “Yes” string if every record is reachable and an encrypted “No” string as soon as one record is impossible.

**What the functions do:**

- `IIl()` initializes the small integer constant array `l` (e.g., `0, 2, 1, 3, 8`).
- `ll()` decrypts the three result strings stored in `I`: two failure strings (likely both “No”/“Ne”) and one success string (likely “Yes”/“Ano”).
- `I(...)`, `l(...)`, and `Il(...)` are string-decryption helpers using XOR, DES, and Blowfish, respectively.
- `lIIl`, `lIl`, `lll`, `IIIl`, and `Ill` are tiny comparison helpers (`>=`, `<`, `<=`, `!= 0`, `== 0`).

**Core logic in `main`:**

1. Read `n` and three arrays `A[]` (time), `B[]` (x), `C[]` (y).
2. For each record `i`:
   - If `i == 0`, compute `dist = |B[0]| + |C[0]|` and `dt = A[0]`.
   - Otherwise, compute `dist = |B[i] - B[i-1]| + |C[i] - C[i-1]|` and `dt = A[i] - A[i-1]`.
   - The record is feasible only if `dist <= dt` **and** `dist` and `dt` have opposite parity (so the excess time can be wasted by back-and-forth moves).
   - If any record fails, output the failure string and exit.
3. If all records pass, output the success string.

So the program is an obfuscated solution to a classic competitive-programming reachability problem on a Manhattan grid.

The program reads an integer N, then N triples (t, x, y). It checks whether a moving point can start at (0, 0) at time 0 and visit each (x, y) exactly at the corresponding time t, moving on the integer grid with one unit per time step (and able to waste time by backtracking).

For the first triple it requires |x| + |y| ≤ t and (|x| + |y|) % 2 == t % 2. For each later triple it compares the differences with the previous one, requiring |x_i − x_{i-1}| + |y_i − y_{i-1}| ≤ t_i − t_{i-1} and matching parity of the sum and time difference. If any check fails it prints "No" and exits; if all pass it prints "Yes".

The obfuscation—renamed variables, fake branches, string encryption, and helper boolean methods—does not change this validation logic.

**Title:** Counting Bounded Integer Triples That Sum to S

**Main goal:**  
Given two integers `K` and `S` read from standard input, the program outputs the number of triples of integers `(X, Y, Z)` such that:

```
0 ≤ X, Y, Z ≤ K   and   X + Y + Z = S
```

**How it works:**

- `main()` reads `K` and `S` and prints `g(S, K)`.
- `f(n, m)` counts pairs of integers `(a, b)` with `0 ≤ a, b ≤ m` and `a + b = n`. It does this by brute force over all possible `a` in `[0, m]` and checking whether `n - a` also lies in `[0, m]`.
- `g(s, k)` computes the desired answer by summing `f(s - x, k)` over all possible values of `x` in `[0, k]`. Effectively, it fixes `X = x`, then counts valid `(Y, Z)` pairs.

The program reads two integers, K and S, from standard input and prints the number of integer triples (x, y, z) such that:

- 0 ≤ x, y, z ≤ K
- x + y + z = S

It computes this by iterating over one variable (i from 0 to K), and for each value it counts how many pairs (j, k) in the same range also satisfy i + j + k = S. Title: Backspace Simulator with Custom Fast Scanner

Main goal: The code reads one whitespace-delimited string from standard input and interprets each uppercase 'B' as a backspace/removal of the most recent character. It then prints the resulting string after all backspaces have been applied.
